entities.name: House of Hohenzollern
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The House of Hohenzollern, originally a Swabian noble family that rose to rule Brandenburg (from 1415), Prussia (from 1618), and ultimately the German Empire (1871-1918), transformed from a minor German principality into Europe's most militaristic great power in 250 years. The Hohenzollerns built the Prussian military state — known for the phrase attributed to Voltaire ('Where some states have an army, the Prussian army has a state') — and under Wilhelm I and Bismarck unified the German states into the German Empire (1871), creating modern Germany.

The dynasty's defining rulers: Frederick the Great (r. 1740-1786) — the paradigmatic 'enlightened despot,' musician, philosopher, and military genius who seized Silesia from Austria (1740), survived the Seven Years' War against France, Austria, Russia, and Sweden simultaneously, and doubled Prussia's size; Otto von Bismarck's master-diplomacy under Wilhelm I (1861-1888) — three wars (Danish War 1864, Austro-Prussian War 1866, Franco-Prussian War 1870-71) in 7 years unified Germany.

Wilhelm II (r. 1888-1918) — aggressive, impulsive, and obsessed with naval expansion — is historians' foremost example of a ruler whose personality shaped world events: his dismissal of Bismarck (1890), his naval arms race with Britain (driving the Anglo-French Entente), and his 'blank check' to Austria in July 1914 contributed directly to WWI. His abdication November 9, 1918 — the same day the German Republic was proclaimed — ended both the dynasty and the German Empire. The house's legacy is thus inseparable from WWI, the German defeat, and the conditions that led to WWII.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The House of Hohenzollern — building Europe's most militaristic state, unifying Germany under Bismarck, and ending in WWI's catastrophe — shaped 20th-century world history more than almost any dynasty: its military culture, unification, and Wilhelm II's role in WWI directly caused the chain that led to the Second World War and the Holocaust.
